entries.consequence: On "ask me first", nothing goes out under your name until you have seen what it is, who gets it, and what happens if it is wrong, and said yes. On "announce only", it goes and then tells you. On "say nothing", things are sent as you without you seeing them at the time, and you would only find them later in the record.
capabilities: On the looser answers, work can go out under your name without you stopping to read it first, so a batch of sends finishes while you are doing something else.
risks: On "say nothing", the first you know of a wrong recipient, a wrong file or a wrong claim is when you go looking in the record, or when the person who received it replies.
Anything sent this way still went out as you, and cannot be unsent.

entries.consequence: A gate is a condition you set: do not send this until I have checked that. This is where you see the ones you have set, add new ones, and clear the ones you are done with.
capabilities: Lets you stop one specific kind of send until a condition you name has been checked, without switching anything else off.
risks: A gate you set and forget keeps holding sends back long after the reason has passed, and the work waits without telling you why unless you come here.

entries.consequence: Scheduled work runs while you are away. This decides whether it may send things out on its own, hold them for you to look at when you are back, or never send at all.
capabilities: On "send it", scheduled work finishes on its own overnight instead of waiting for you to come back and release it.
risks: Nobody sees the send before it happens, so a mistake made at 3am reaches its destination at 3am.
You are not there to notice that the run went wrong in a way the checks did not catch.

externalStep.whatItDoes: Lets Windows run your scheduled work when ToolsEnabled is not open, by registering it as a scheduled task once.
capabilitiesGained: Scheduled work runs at the time you set it, even if this program is closed or the computer has been restarted since.
A subsystem that crashes can start itself again instead of staying down until you notice.
risks: Something you set up runs on this computer at times when nobody is watching it, which is the whole point and also the whole risk.
A task registered once stays registered until you remove it, including after you have stopped using the feature.
externalStep.frequencyBecause: Registering work that runs while you are signed out needs a Windows privilege called SeBatchLogonRight, and only an administrator has it. That is true on every Windows machine at its default settings; there is no configuration in which an ordinary account can do it. It is one step per piece of scheduled work, not one per run. Derived from what Windows requires, not from whether a prompt was seen on any particular computer.

steps.do: Open Windows PowerShell as an administrator: right-click the Start button, choose "Terminal (Admin)", and approve the Windows prompt.
steps.why: Registering a task that runs whether or not you are signed in is an administrator action. This product cannot do it, does not ask Windows to let it, and does not weaken any Windows security setting to avoid the prompt. You approve it yourself, and you can close the window and change nothing. If Windows does not ask you at all, that is because the administrator prompt has been turned off on this computer, which is worth knowing on its own.

steps.do: Run the registrar command the product prints for the work you scheduled. It prints the exact line; it never runs it.
steps.why: You can read the command before you run it, which you cannot do for something a program runs on your behalf.
Nothing else needs it, and an administrator prompt left open is its own small risk.

externalStep.verify: Run Get-ScheduledTask and see the task listed by name. Your scheduled work then also runs with this program closed.
externalStep.withoutIt: The setting stays on and saves, and scheduled work still runs normally while ToolsEnabled is open. It will not run when the program is closed or after a restart, and the schedule says so rather than reporting a run that never happened.

entries.consequence: With this on, before the assistant sends, uploads, or submits anything as you, it first goes and looks at where it is sending and reads what is already there. Turn it off and it will act on what your own computer remembers instead, which is how the same paper gets submitted twice, or how a newer version already sitting at the destination gets replaced by an older one.
capabilities: Off, sends complete faster and work when the destination is temporarily unreachable, because nothing has to be read back first.
risks: Off, the assistant acts on what this computer remembers about the destination, which is how the same paper gets submitted twice, or a newer version already sitting there gets replaced by an older one.

entries.consequence: The assistant can draft things for you, but they only go out as your work once you say they are yours. This decides whether you say that for each item, or once for a whole project or destination.
capabilities: Saying yes once for a whole project or destination means you are not asked again for every individual item.
risks: A single yes then covers items you have not seen, including ones drafted after you gave it.

entries.consequence: Different places expect different file names. Add a destination here and the assistant will match the naming style already used there instead of inventing one.
capabilities: Files arrive at each destination named the way that destination already names things, so nothing has to be renamed by hand afterwards.
risks: A pattern that no longer matches what a destination expects produces names that look deliberate and are wrong, which is harder to notice than an obviously odd name.

entries.consequence: Refuse is the shipped setting. The assistant refuses to send anything outward that it cannot tie back to a request of yours, so nothing goes out unaccountably. If you do not keep a list of requests at all, this will make outward work impossible for a reason you cannot see, which is why this setting is here. Warn lets the send proceed and marks it. Off removes the check, and with it the only thing tying what leaves this machine to something you asked for.
capabilities: On "warn" or "off", sends go through even when they cannot be tied back to a request you recorded, which is what you want if you do not keep a list of requests at all.
risks: Off, nothing outward is accountable to anything you asked for, so there is no way afterwards to answer "who wanted this sent?"

Off removes the check, and with it the only thing tying what leaves this machine to something you asked for.

entries.consequence: This decides whose name your assistants act under, and nothing else. On "not authorized" they will stop at anything that would be done as you — creating an account in your name, registering a business, publishing under your publisher identity — and ask you to do it or to authorize it. On "authorized for my business" they stop asking that question and proceed, but only for the business you have named, and only for the things you have not reserved on the next setting. This never widens what they are allowed to do: everything they could not do before, they still cannot do. It changes who the action is attributed to, not what actions are possible.
capabilities: Authorized, assistants can finish things that only work when done as you: creating an account in your name, registering a business, publishing under your byline.
risks: Anything done under this is legally and practically yours, whether or not you saw it first.
The list of things reserved for you is the only remaining line between an assistant and acting as you; if that list is thin, this setting is doing a lot of work on its own.

default: Approving any purchase or spending any money
Anything needing your passport or government ID
entries.consequence: These are the things you keep for yourself even when your assistants are authorized to act as you. They will do all the work up to each one and then stop and hand it to you — the shopping list gets assembled but you approve it, the post gets written but you press post. Anything you remove from this list, they will do themselves without asking. Anything you add, they will prepare and then wait on. If you authorize them to act as you and empty this list entirely, you have given them a blank cheque, so the product refuses to treat an empty list as a grant.
capabilities: Lets assistants stay authorized to act as you while still stopping dead at the specific acts you keep for yourself.
risks: Anything you take off this list becomes something an authorized assistant may do as you, immediately and without a further prompt.
entries.enforcedBy: config/owner-authorization.json carries the stored reservations; src/lib/owner-authorization.js refuses to render a grant that reserves nothing; purchase.request enqueues for your approval and never spends; and the purchase reservation is enforced on the spend path itself by src/lib/purchase-authority.js, which src/lib/providers/pay.js calls before it records any charge, so a spend that names no line you approved is refused rather than merely discouraged.

entries.consequence: This is where your agents come to find you when they need an answer. Point it somewhere you do not actually watch and the work quietly stops, or worse, the agent guesses. Whatever you pick, passwords and keys are never requested this way; those always go through the secure vault prompt.
capabilities: Fixes one place your agents come to find you, so a question does not sit unnoticed somewhere you never look.
risks: Point this at somewhere you do not actually watch and work quietly stops, or the agent gives up waiting and guesses.

entries.consequence: Before the assistant stops and waits, it checks whether you have said anything. Turn it off and it can go quiet while a message from you is still sitting there unread. You will not get an error; it will just look like nothing is happening until it wakes up on its own.
capabilities: On, an assistant picks up an answer you already sent instead of stopping to ask for it again.
risks: Off, it can go quiet while a message from you sits unread. You get no error; it just looks like nothing is happening.

entries.consequence: When an assistant hits something it cannot do, it stops. This decides whether you hear about it straight away, at your next check-in, or only when you go looking.
capabilities: On "queue quietly", you are not interrupted every time something stops, and you read the whole list when you are ready.
risks: A job that stopped an hour ago has been doing nothing for an hour, and on the quieter settings you do not find out until you look.

entries.default: Pause only when it truly needs me
entries.consequence: This decides whether your agents stop and wait for you. On the most hands-off setting they approve their own next steps and keep working while you sleep, much faster, but work can travel a long way in the wrong direction before you next look at it. On the most cautious setting nothing meaningful happens without your say-so, but agents sit idle every time you step away.
capabilities: On the hands-off end, agents approve their own next steps and keep working while you sleep, which is much faster.
risks: Work can travel a long way in the wrong direction before anyone reads it, and undoing a night of confident wrong work is slower than the night was.
options: Pause only when it truly needs me

entries.consequence: When you ask for something new, this decides how much the assistant checks what you meant before it starts building. Set it to just start and you get motion immediately, at the risk that it read your request more broadly or more narrowly than you intended and you find out after the work is done. Set it to always confirm and you answer a couple of questions up front on every request, which is slower but means the first attempt is aimed at the right thing.
capabilities: On "just start" you get motion immediately, with no back-and-forth before anything is built.
risks: The assistant may have read your request more broadly or more narrowly than you meant, and you find that out from the finished thing.

entries.consequence: Sometimes you say something about one particular case and the assistant writes it down as a rule about everything. This catches that. On the default you get a visible mark on any rule that came out broader than what you actually said, so you can fix it in a moment. On the strictest setting that rule does not take effect at all until you confirm it, safer, but work that depends on it waits for you. Turned off, the broadened rule quietly takes effect and you will only notice it later, in the work it steers.
capabilities: Catches the moment a remark about one case gets written down as a rule about everything, before that rule starts steering later work.
risks: Off, a rule broader than anything you said keeps applying, and its effects look like the assistant’s own judgement rather than like a rule you can go and delete.

entries.consequence: Words like finish, launch, done and wire up can mean very different amounts of work. With this on, the agent tells you which meaning it went with and what it is deliberately leaving out, before it starts. It does not stop and wait, it just says so. With it off you get shorter messages and find out what it decided by looking at what it built.
capabilities: You see which meaning of a word like "finish" or "launch" the agent went with, and what it is deliberately leaving out, before it starts.
risks: Almost none. It adds a short paragraph before work starts and does not slow anything down or stop to ask.

entries.consequence: Before doing something consequential the assistant checks which of your rules apply. This decides how much of that check you see: nothing, a single line, or the full list. It changes what is shown to you and never whether the check happens.
capabilities: On "full", you can see exactly which of your rules were consulted before a consequential action.
risks: None to what the assistant may do. This changes only how much of the check you are shown, never whether the check happens.

entries.consequence: Everything you have told your assistants, merged into one list, with each line showing which of your instructions it came from and what it replaced.
capabilities: Shows everything your assistants are currently following as one list, with the origin of each line and what it replaced.
risks: None. This reads and shows; it changes nothing on its own.

entries.consequence: On, every turn started by ToolsEnabled includes the complete current Ledger rules that apply to that agent: global, session, inherited tree and conversation rules. If the rules cannot be read completely or do not fit, the turn does not start. Off, the existing rule refresh behavior remains. This ensures the rules reach the assistant; it cannot prove that the assistant understands or follows them.
capabilities: Supplies all applicable active rules on every turn, including continued work and agents without an assigned role.
Prevents a turn from starting with missing, stale or shortened rules.
risks: Repeating all rules uses more context and can increase allowance use.
A turn cannot start if the rules cannot be read or exceed the assistant's input limit. Independently started agents are not covered.
entries.enforcedBy: src/lib/rules-turn-snapshot.js reads this setting and the complete canonical rule snapshot; desktop shell/agent-host.cjs includes and rechecks it before every enabled provider turn.

entries.consequence: Require work assignments and reports to use tasks. Direct agent messages are refused even when Agent comms is on. Task filing, assignment and checkpoints remain subject to existing role and permission limits.
capabilities: Keep assignments and progress in persistent task records.
risks: Direct messages between agents are unavailable while this is on.
entries.enforcedBy: src/lib/agent-delegation-policy.js; local and cross-machine provider send boundaries; tools/agent-msg.js before message preparation.

entries.consequence: Allow agents to send messages. Off refuses new local and cross-computer sends while preserving existing messages and task records. Assign work only through tasks takes precedence when enabled.
capabilities: Control new agent-to-agent messages without disabling task checkpoints.
risks: Agents must use task records to coordinate when direct messages are unavailable.
entries.enforcedBy: src/lib/agent-delegation-policy.js; local and cross-machine provider send boundaries; tools/agent-msg.js before message preparation.

entries.consequence: Choose Instant to deliver agent messages during active turns when the runtime supports additional input, Timer to collect messages for the selected interval, or End of turn to wait for completion. The courier never stops an active turn. Unsupported runtimes keep messages queued for the next boundary.
capabilities: Receive agent reports while work continues.
Collect incoming agent reports and deliver them together after your chosen interval.
risks: Instant delivery can change the focus of work in progress.
A runtime without live input delivers at the next turn boundary.
entries.enforcedBy: src/lib/agent-message-delivery.js reads this choice for the desktop shell/agent-host.cjs courier; shell/agent-message-delivery.cjs chooses steering, queued delivery, or the next turn.

entries.consequence: When Timer is selected, collect messages for this many seconds starting from the first queued message. New arrivals do not extend the timer.
capabilities: Control how often a batch of agent messages is delivered.
risks: Longer intervals delay incoming results and questions.
entries.enforcedBy: src/lib/agent-message-delivery.js supplies the timer to the desktop shell/agent-host.cjs courier.

entries.consequence: Who may add a standing rule to your ledger. Ledger page only: you add rules by hand on the Ledger page, and a /Request typed in a chat is refused with a note pointing you there. Ledger page and /Request: you add rules on the Ledger page or by typing /Request, /RequestSession, /RequestTree or /RequestThread in a chat. Agents too: as well as both of those, your agents may turn something you said into a rule, filed under the agent's name; the two settings nested below decide whether an unsure agent asks first and whether an agent's rule waits for your approval. In the first two choices agents neither file rules nor ask you whether to; they carry on with the work. The reset buttons on the Ledger page are yours in every choice.
capabilities: One choice decides every door into the rules ledger: the page, the chat command, and your agents.
risks: Agents too: an offhand remark can become a rule that steers later sessions until you find it on the Ledger page and remove it.
Ledger page only: a rule typed as /Request in a chat is refused, so a habit of typing rules in chat stops working until you change this.
entries.enforcedBy: src/lib/r-ledger-agent-gate.js reads this row for whether agents may file (through the rules.capture_spoken switch that src/lib/settings.js keeps in step with it) and whether the /Request commands are offered; the desktop shell/agent-host.cjs fileStandingRequest refuses a /Request typed in a chat when the choice is Ledger page only

entries.consequence: The older on/off form of "Who adds standing rules": it reads on when that choice is Agents too and off otherwise, and choosing there is what changes it. Your agents can notice when you say something meant to last — "always ask before spending money", "from now on keep it short" — and write it down as a standing rule in your own words. Off: only you file rules, by typing /Request. On: the agent decides when something you said is a rule and files it, marked as filed by that agent; the chat shows you a line saying what was filed and where, and every later session reads it until you edit or delete the entry by hand. When an agent is unsure it suggests the rule instead and you accept or decline it. This covers the standing-rule ledgers only — your agents' durable notes, research findings, tasks and messages have their own tools and are not changed here. At the Guided level agents only read, so nothing is filed either way.
capabilities: You say a thing once, in your own words, and it keeps applying — no command to remember.
risks: On, an offhand remark can become a rule that steers every later session until you find it in the rules panel and delete it by hand.
An agent can only name the scope keys it was shown, but a mistaken key puts a rule on the wrong circle until you see it there.
entries.enforcedBy: src/lib/r-ledger-agent-gate.js

entries.consequence: When your agent is not sure you meant a standing rule, or not sure who it covers, it files nothing and ends its reply with one short question; your yes files your original sentence. Off: the agent uses the narrowest reading and says so.
capabilities: A doubtful remark never becomes a rule behind your back: the agent asks once, briefly, and waits for your yes.
risks: On, you will be asked a short question now and then, and a rule you did mean waits on file until you answer it.
entries.enforcedBy: src/lib/r-ledger-agent-gate.js

entries.consequence: When an agent files a rule from your words, it waits on the Ledger page until you approve it. Until then, no agent treats it as in force. Off, an agent-filed rule counts as soon as it is filed; you can still edit or delete it.
capabilities: Nothing an agent wrote down from your words counts as a rule until you have looked at it and said yes.
risks: On, a rule you did mean waits on the Ledger page, and agents work without it until you approve it.
entries.enforcedBy: src/lib/r-ledger-agent-gate.js agentFiledNeedsApprovalOf() is what reads this row, under the same provenance rule as its two siblings; src/lib/owner-request-store.js fileRequest asks it and files an agent’s rule as proposed rather than active when the answer is yes

entries.consequence: Assistants can notice that a rule is causing trouble and suggest a change. With this on, suggestions land in a list for you to accept or throw away. They never take effect on their own, and nothing an assistant writes changes a rule you set.
capabilities: Assistants can point out that a rule is causing trouble and offer a replacement, which is how a bad rule gets found.
risks: Very little: proposals land in a list and never take effect on their own. The cost is a list to review.

entries.consequence: When something goes wrong, the system can work out what rule would have prevented it. Off means it only reports. Propose means suggested rules wait for you. Auto means it applies them itself within the limits it is allowed, and tells you what it changed. Your own instructions are never rewritten automatically in any position.
capabilities: On "auto", a rule that would have prevented a failure is applied without waiting for you, so the same failure does not recur tonight.
risks: The system is then writing the rules it follows, and a rule inferred from one bad night can be wrong about every night after it.

entries.consequence: This is the list of every rule that got written down automatically because you said something that sounded like a standing instruction. Come here to see what was captured; to correct anything it misheard or remove something you only meant for that one moment, open the ledger file and edit it by hand — no tool rewrites your words. Skip this list and a rule from an offhand remark keeps quietly steering your agents' work, and you would only notice from its effects, not from anything telling you it happened.
capabilities: Lets you see, correct and delete every rule that got written down automatically from something you said.
risks: None from reading it. Deleting a rule here takes effect immediately, which is the point.

entries.consequence: This decides how closely the managing agent watches the workers. On the cheapest setting it reads only each worker's own summary of what it did, rather than the actual work, much less expensive, but a worker that reports success while producing something wrong will not be caught until you look yourself. On the most thorough setting it double-checks the real output and you pay noticeably more. No setting will let it stop checking altogether, because that is not a cheaper product, it is a broken one.
capabilities: On "minimize cost", the lead reads each worker’s own summary instead of the work itself, which costs considerably less.
risks: A worker that reports success it did not achieve is believed, and nothing else is looking.

entries.consequence: Decides whether your lead assistant does the work itself or hands it to other assistants and stays back to direct them. Doing it itself is simpler and easier to follow. Handing it off gets more done at once, but the lead is then reporting on work it did not watch happen.
capabilities: Handing work off gets more done at once, because several assistants work in parallel.
risks: The lead is then judging work it did not do, from reports rather than from the thing itself, and a run is harder to follow after the fact.

entries.consequence: A checkpoint is a save point taken before assistants start changing your files. Take them less often and there is less clutter in your project history, but if a batch of assistants makes a mess there is no clean moment to rewind to; you keep whatever state they left behind.
capabilities: Taking checkpoints less often leaves less clutter in your project history.
risks: If a batch of assistants makes a mess, there is no clean moment to go back to, and the mess has to be untangled by hand.

entries.consequence: Turn this on and the assistant that reviews your code starts changing it instead of only telling you what it found. Problems get fixed without waiting for you, but the only thing that was checking the other assistants' work is now producing work of its own, and nothing checks that.
capabilities: Problems found in review get fixed immediately instead of waiting in a list for you.
risks: The only thing that was independently checking the other assistants is now one of them, so a mistake it makes has nothing left watching for it.

entries.consequence: Decides when the reviewing assistant looks at new work: as it appears, only when you ask, or only before something is merged.
capabilities: On "continuous", a problem is found while the work that caused it is still fresh and small.
risks: Reviewing only when you ask means problems accumulate quietly until something asks for them.

entries.consequence: The assistant can either open and click through web pages itself, or start up a helper to do it. Handing it off keeps the main assistant free to carry on with your work and keeps a separate record of everything that was clicked. Doing it itself is quicker for one small lookup, but it ties the assistant up until the browsing finishes, and the web work gets mixed into its main train of thought instead of being kept apart.
capabilities: Handing web pages to a helper keeps the main assistant working on your task, and keeps a separate record of everything that was clicked.
risks: A second program is driving a browser on this computer, and whatever is signed in to that browser is reachable from it.

externalStep.whatItDoes: Installs the browser the helper drives.
capabilitiesGained: Assistants can open and click through web pages instead of stopping at anything that needs a browser.
risks: A browser under program control can reach any site your saved sign-ins reach.

steps.do: Install the browser the helper uses, from its own installer.
steps.why: This product does not install software on your computer.

externalStep.verify: Ask an assistant to open a page. It reports the page title instead of reporting that no browser is available.

entries.consequence: Require your approval for each purchase amount recorded in the spending ledger. Turning this off also removes the purchase reservation; your other reservations and daily spending limit remain in effect. This control does not execute payments.

risks: When approval is off, assistants can record spending without a new local confirmation for each amount.
